topic.title: CodeMender & AI Threat Defense
topic.summary: 4 AI Threat Defense stages (CodeMender in Remediate), importing external SAST findings (cm report import -> cm verify -> cm fix), 7 languages, Gemini Flash (--model), Indirect PI vs Tool Poisoning.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.8 CodeMender | Self-Test #6 & Trigger #11 | M2S1 Slide 44
questions.q: What are the four stages of the Google AI Threat Defense framework (in order), and which stage does CodeMender's 'fix' capability belong to?
options: Prepare → Scan and Prioritize → Remediate → Monitor; CodeMender's fix work belongs to Remediate (Stage 3)
Discover → Assess → Migrate → Optimize; CodeMender belongs to Assess
Register → Discover → Govern → Orchestrate; CodeMender belongs to Govern
Span → Trace → Session → Task; CodeMender belongs to Span
questions.why: Per §1.8 & Self-Test #6 (M2S1 Slide 44): The four AI Threat Defense stages are Prepare → Scan and Prioritize → Remediate → Monitor. CodeMender's patch generation, testing, and fixing happen in Stage 3: Remediate.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.8 CodeMender | Trigger #11 | M2S1 Slides 47–53
questions.q: A security team already uses an existing third-party SAST scanner and does not want to rip and replace it. How can they adopt CodeMender?
options: CodeMender can import external SAST findings (via 'cm report import') and go straight to verify and fix, leaving the existing scanner in place
They must uninstall their existing SAST tool because CodeMender can only act on its own scan findings
They must first route all findings through Security Command Center Enterprise and wait 30 days
CodeMender cannot verify or patch vulnerabilities found by external tools
questions.why: Per §1.8 & Trigger #11: CodeMender can import external findings ('cm report import') and proceed directly to 'cm verify' and 'cm fix', leaving the customer's existing scanner in place.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.8 CodeMender | Trigger #11 | M2S1 Slide 50
questions.q: Which set of CLI commands is provided by CodeMender?
options: cm find, cm verify, cm fix, cm report (and cm report import for external findings)
cm build, cm deploy, cm scale, cm billing
adk scan, adk patch, adk push, adk rollback
gcloud armor scan, gcloud armor fix
questions.why: Per §1.8 & Trigger #11: CodeMender's CLI commands are 'cm find', 'cm verify', 'cm fix', 'cm report', and 'cm report import'.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.8 CodeMender | Trigger #11 | M2S1 Slide 49
questions.q: Which 7 programming languages are officially supported by CodeMender?
options: C/C++, Go, Java, Python, Ruby, Rust, and TypeScript
COBOL, Fortran, Pascal, Assembly, Perl, PHP, and Swift
Python and JavaScript only
SQL, HTML, CSS, YAML, JSON, Markdown, and Bash
questions.why: Per §1.8 & Trigger #11: CodeMender supports 7 languages: C/C++, Go, Java, Python, Ruby, Rust, and TypeScript.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.8 CodeMender | Trigger #11 | M2S1 Slide 51
questions.q: Which model does CodeMender use by default, and how can a developer override it?
options: Defaults to a Gemini Flash model; override it using the --model flag with a supported model identifier
Defaults to Gemini Ultra; can only be changed by filing a Google Cloud support ticket
Defaults to a local CPU regex engine; cannot use Gemini models
Defaults to PaLM 2; override by editing /etc/hosts
questions.why: Per §1.8 & Trigger #11: CodeMender defaults to a Gemini Flash model, and users can override it with the '--model' CLI flag and a supported model identifier. Watch out for the trap 'Model can only be changed via a support ticket.'

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §5 Trigger #11 (Swapped-Definition Trap) | M2S2 Slide 5
questions.q: In agentic security threat modeling, what is the difference between Indirect Prompt Injection and Tool Poisoning?
options: Indirect Prompt Injection hides malicious instructions inside external data/documents the agent reads; Tool Poisoning occurs when a compromised MCP server or tool returns malicious outputs or metadata
Tool Poisoning is when a user types a jailbreak directly into chat; Indirect Prompt Injection is when an MCP server binary is infected
Both terms refer exclusively to DDoS attacks on Cloud Load Balancing
Indirect Prompt Injection only affects images, while Tool Poisoning only affects audio
questions.why: Per Trigger #11 (M2S2 Slide 5): Indirect Prompt Injection = malicious instructions embedded inside external content/documents the agent reads. Tool Poisoning = compromised MCP servers or tools returning malicious outputs/instructions.

questions.q: Why does CodeMender include a dedicated verification step ('cm verify') between finding/importing a vulnerability and generating a patch ('cm fix')?
options: To confirm whether the vulnerability is actually exploitable in the codebase and filter out SAST false positives before engineering a fix
To bill the customer double for input tokens
To upload the source code to a public GitHub repository
To convert all unit tests into Markdown files
questions.why: Traditional SAST tools generate high false-positive noise; CodeMender verifies that findings are genuinely exploitable in context before generating and testing remediation patches.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §6.4 Offensive AI Metrics | M2S1 Slides 18, 41–43
questions.q: According to the Module 2 Threat Intelligence slides (M2S1 Slides 18, 41–43), how has offensive AI impacted vulnerability exploitation speed and CVE coverage?
options: Average Time-to-Exploit dropped to 1.6 days (down from 1.3 years in 2020), with 10x faster recon and 85% CVE coverage for generating working PoC exploits
Time-to-Exploit increased to 5 years because AI models refuse security prompts
Offensive AI only affects 1% of CVEs and requires 6 months of manual tuning per exploit
Annual CVEs dropped by 80% since 2020
questions.why: Per §6.4 (M2S1 Slides 18, 41–43): Offensive AI achieves 10x faster recon, 85% CVE coverage (working PoCs from CVE descriptions), <30s autonomous stage handoffs, and 1.6 days average Time-to-Exploit (down from 1.3 years in 2020) vs 20–70 day human patching timelines.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §6.4 Secure Agentic TDD Lab | M2S1 Slides 60–62
questions.q: In the Module 2 Secure Agentic TDD Lab (M2S1 Slides 60–62), what is the 4-step defense-in-depth loop when an coding agent accidentally introduces a hardcoded credential?
options: 1. CONTEXT.md workspace rules → 2. Custom Semgrep rule → 3. Git pre-commit hook blocks the commit → 4. Antigravity agent reads the error and self-corrects the code
1. Deploy to prod → 2. Wait for user bug report → 3. Roll back VM → 4. Delete repo
1. Disable Git → 2. Email security team → 3. Run Basic SDP → 4. Reboot Cloudtop
1. Floor settings → 2. Agent Registry → 3. BigQuery ObjectRef → 4. Provisioned Throughput
questions.why: Per §6.4 (M2S1 Slides 60–62): The Secure Agentic TDD loop combines preventative rules (CONTEXT.md) with deterministic enforcement (Semgrep + Git pre-commit hook blocking the mock credential), triggering the Antigravity agent to analyze the hook error and self-correct.

questions.docRef: Elevate Capstone Prep (Oct 7-8).md — §1.8 CodeMender | M2S1 Slide 48
questions.q: How does CodeMender handle patch safety and developer governance during the Remediate stage?
options: It generates candidate patches, validates them against tests to ensure no regressions, and presents them for human developer review and approval before committing
It force-pushes unreviewed binary patches directly to the production main branch without running tests
It deletes vulnerable files from production without creating a replacement patch
It only outputs a PDF report and cannot generate code diffs
questions.why: Per §1.8: CodeMender generates patches, runs tests to verify the fix doesn't break functionality, and keeps a human developer in the loop to review and approve the patch before committing.
